quiz.q: In a three-point cross, the parental classes are ABC and abc, and the rarest classes are AbC and aBc. Which gene lies in the middle?
choices: Cannot be determined without recombination frequencies
quiz.why: A double crossover flips only the middle marker relative to the parental arrangement, and B is the allele that changed position. Map distances are needed to place the genes numerically but not to identify the order.

quiz.q: Two loci sit 40 map units apart on the same chromosome. What recombination frequency would you observe?
choices: 0 percent, because they are on the same chromosome
50 percent, since anything on one chromosome is linked
About 40 percent, close to but below the 50 percent unlinked ceiling
quiz.why: Map units are defined as percent recombinants, so 40 map units means about 40 percent, which is detectably below the 50 percent ceiling. Being on the same chromosome does not force linkage when the distance is large.

quiz.q: A newborn has a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, hypotonia, and an endocardial cushion defect. Which karyotype is most likely?
quiz.why: This is the classic Down syndrome picture, and 40 to 50 percent have congenital heart disease, often endocardial cushion defects. Trisomy 18 gives clenched hands and rocker-bottom feet, and 45,X occurs only in females.

quiz.q: A couple has had four first-trimester miscarriages. Both partners are healthy. What is the most appropriate genetic evaluation?
choices: Trinucleotide repeat testing in the mother
Parental karyotypes to look for a balanced translocation
quiz.why: A healthy balanced translocation carrier produces unbalanced gametes, and recurrent pregnancy loss is the classic presentation. Carrier screening looks for recessive alleles, which cause disease in liveborn children rather than repeated early loss.

quiz.q: A tall 27-year-old man presents for infertility. He has small firm testes, gynecomastia, and low testosterone. What karyotype is expected?
quiz.why: This is Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY, which affects about 1 in 600 male births and is often found during infertility workup. 45,X is Turner syndrome in females and t(9;22) is the acquired Philadelphia chromosome of chronic myeloid leukemia.

quiz.q: An infant has a conotruncal cardiac defect, hypocalcemic seizures, recurrent infections, and a cleft palate. Which abnormality explains this?
quiz.why: Thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia with outflow tract defects is the 22q11.2 deletion, DiGeorge syndrome. Cri-du-chat from 5p deletion gives a catlike cry without immune or calcium problems, and trisomy 13 presents with midline defects and very early death.

quiz.q: A recessive disease has an affected frequency of 1 in 1,600. What is the carrier frequency?
quiz.why: q^2 = 1/1600 gives q = 0.025, and carriers are about 2q = 0.05, which is 1 in 20. The 1 in 40 answer is q itself, the single most common slip in these problems.

quiz.q: Red-green color blindness affects 8 percent of males in a population. What percentage of females is expected to be affected?
quiz.why: For X-linked traits the male frequency equals q, so q = 0.08 and affected females are q^2 = 0.0064, or 0.64 percent. Using 8 or 16 percent treats females like hemizygous males or doubles the allele frequency incorrectly.

quiz.q: Tay-Sachs disease is far more common among Ashkenazi Jews than in the general population. Which force best explains this?
choices: Nonrandom mating at a single locus
quiz.why: A population descended from a small ancestral group carries whatever allele mix that group happened to have, which is the founder effect. Malaria resistance explains sickle cell, not Tay-Sachs, and mutation rates do not vary that much between populations.

quiz.q: A couple whose first child was born with a neural tube defect asks about recurrence risk. What is the best estimate and reasoning?
choices: 25 percent, since it is autosomal recessive
50 percent, since it is autosomal dominant
Less than 1 percent, since it is sporadic
About 3 to 5 percent, since it is a multifactorial threshold trait
quiz.why: Neural tube defects are multifactorial with continuous liability, giving first-degree relatives roughly 3 to 5 percent recurrence. Mendelian fractions like 25 or 50 percent do not apply to threshold traits.

quiz.q: Height has a heritability of about 0.8 in a population. What does this mean?
choices: 80 percent of any one person's height is genetic
80 percent of the variation in height in that population is attributable to genetic variation
80 percent of people inherit height from one parent
Nutrition changes height by at most 20 percent
quiz.why: Heritability is a population-level ratio of variances and says nothing about an individual or about the effect of an intervention. The other options all misapply a population statistic to a single person or to causation.

quiz.q: A 23-year-old with no risk factors receives a positive NIPT result for trisomy 18. What should she be told?
choices: The diagnosis is confirmed and she should be referred immediately
The test should simply be repeated in a month
This is a screening result whose predictive value is low at her risk level, and CVS or amniocentesis is needed to confirm
NIPT cannot detect trisomy 18 at all
quiz.why: NIPT detects the common trisomies well but positive predictive value falls with low prior risk, so a diagnostic karyotype must follow. Repeating a screen cannot turn it into a diagnosis, and NIPT does screen for trisomy 18.

quiz.q: A patient with a drug-eluting stent has recurrent in-stent thrombosis on clopidogrel. Genotyping shows CYP2C19 poor metabolizer status. What is the best explanation?
choices: Clopidogrel accumulates to toxic levels and causes platelet activation
CYP2C19 clears clopidogrel faster, lowering its concentration
Clopidogrel is a prodrug that CYP2C19 must activate, so poor metabolizers get little antiplatelet effect
quiz.why: Without activation the drug cannot block P2Y12, so an alternative such as prasugrel or ticagrelor is used. The accumulation and faster-clearance answers reverse the direction of the metabolic problem.

quiz.q: Which test is required before a patient starts abacavir?
quiz.why: HLA-B*5701 carriers can develop a fatal abacavir hypersensitivity reaction, so screening is mandatory. TPMT applies to thiopurines, CYP2D6 to codeine, and HFE to hemochromatosis.

quiz.q: A patient worries that a Huntington test result could be used against her. Which statement about GINA is accurate?
choices: It protects against all forms of insurance discrimination
It prohibits health insurers and employers from using genetic information, but does not cover life, disability or long-term care insurance
It applies only to already symptomatic patients
It requires disclosure of results to the patient's primary insurer
quiz.why: GINA of 2008 covers health coverage and employment with a small-employer exemption, leaving life, disability and long-term care policies outside its reach. Claiming complete protection is the most harmful error here because it affects the patient's decision to test.

quiz.q: A newborn's heel-stick screen returns positive for cystic fibrosis. What does that result mean?
choices: The infant has cystic fibrosis and treatment should begin
The infant is a carrier and needs no follow-up
The screen must be repeated at one year of age
The infant is in a higher-risk group and needs confirmatory sweat chloride or genetic testing
quiz.why: Newborn screening sorts a population into risk groups and never diagnoses on its own, so confirmation is required before treatment or reassurance. Calling a positive screen a diagnosis and dismissing it as carrier status are opposite errors with the same root.

scenarios.title: Problem set: reading a pedigree and computing recurrence risk
scenarios.intro:
Your instructor puts a four-generation pedigree on the board and hands you a worksheet.

Generation I: an unaffected couple. Generation II: four siblings, three unaffected, one affected male. Generation III: the unaffected sisters from II each have children; two of their sons are affected and none of their daughters are. Generation IV: the affected male from generation III has two daughters, both unaffected, and one son, unaffected.

The disease causes progressive proximal muscle weakness beginning around age `4`, with wheelchair use by the early teens. You are asked to name the pattern, assign genotypes, and quote a recurrence risk.

steps.prompt: Every affected person in the pedigree is male, and they are connected to each other through unaffected women. What is your first move?

choices.text: Check whether any affected father has an affected son, since that single observation excludes X-linked inheritance
choices.feedback: Correct, and it is the fastest discriminator on the page. The affected man in generation III has an unaffected son, which is consistent with X-linked recessive rather than against it.

choices.text: Count affected males versus females and call it X-linked recessive immediately
choices.feedback: The male excess is a real clue, but autosomal recessive disease can look male-heavy by chance in a small family. Confirm with transmission pattern before committing.

choices.text: Assume autosomal dominant because affected people appear in three generations
choices.feedback: Look again. The affected people are not the children of affected parents, and the connecting relatives are unaffected women. That is transmission through carriers, not dominance.

steps.prompt: You settle on X-linked recessive, and the clinical picture fits Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Assign genotypes. What can you say with certainty about the mothers of the two affected boys in generation III?

choices.text: They each have a 1/2 chance of being carriers
choices.feedback: That is the prior risk for a sister of a carrier before she has children. Once she has an affected son, the uncertainty is gone.

choices.text: They are obligate carriers, X^A X^a, since each has an affected son and is herself unaffected
choices.feedback: Right. An affected son inherited his only X from his mother, so she must carry the allele. 'Obligate carrier' means the pedigree forces the genotype without any testing.

choices.text: They must be affected but with milder disease
choices.feedback: Carriers can occasionally show mild findings from skewed X-inactivation, but the pedigree marks them unaffected and the genotype conclusion does not depend on symptoms.

steps.prompt: One of those obligate carrier mothers is pregnant again with an unknown fetal sex. What is the risk that this pregnancy results in an affected child?

choices.text: 1/2, since half her children get the mutant X
choices.feedback: Half her children receive the mutant X, but only the males are affected by it. You have skipped the sex step.

choices.text: 1/4, because there is a 1/2 chance of a son and a 1/2 chance that son receives the mutant X
choices.feedback: Correct. Multiply the two independent events: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 affected per pregnancy. If you already know it is a boy, the risk becomes 1/2.

choices.text: 1/8, since three things must happen
choices.feedback: Only two independent events matter here: the sex of the fetus and which X the mother transmits. There is no third factor to multiply in.

choices.text: 1/4 overall, and 1/2 if the fetus is known to be male
choices.feedback: Exactly the right framing. Conditioning on what you already know is the entire skill in recurrence-risk problems.

steps.prompt: The affected man in generation III asks about his own children. He has two daughters and one son, all unaffected. What do you tell him?

choices.text: All of his daughters are obligate carriers, and none of his sons can be affected through him
choices.feedback: Correct. He has one X and must give it to every daughter, so all are carriers. His sons get his Y, so he cannot transmit the disease to them at all.

choices.text: Each daughter has a 1/2 chance of carrying the allele
choices.feedback: That is what you would say about a carrier mother. An affected father has only the mutant X to give, so the probability is 1, not 1/2.

choices.text: His son should still be tested, since he could be a silent carrier
choices.feedback: Males are hemizygous — one X, no carrier state. An unaffected son of an affected father did not receive the allele.

steps.prompt: One of the unaffected sisters in generation II has never had children and wants to know her own carrier risk. Her mother in generation I is an obligate carrier, since she had an affected son. How do you work it?

choices.text: Her prior risk is 1/2, since her carrier mother transmits the mutant X to half of her daughters
choices.feedback: Correct starting point. With no children and no testing, 1/2 is the honest number, and carrier testing or family-variant testing can resolve it.

choices.text: Her risk is 2/3, the same as an unaffected sibling in autosomal recessive disease
choices.feedback: That 2/3 comes from removing the aa box in an autosomal recessive square. Here she cannot be affected regardless, so there is nothing to rescale.

choices.text: Her risk is 1/4, matching the per-pregnancy risk figure
choices.feedback: The 1/4 is a risk to an offspring, not a genotype probability for an adult woman. Keep the two kinds of numbers separate.

choices.text: Her risk is 1/2, and it would drop substantially after several unaffected sons
choices.feedback: Both halves are right. Bayesian updating on unaffected sons lowers the posterior carrier probability, which is exactly how counselors refine these numbers.

steps.prompt: Last question on the worksheet: the family asks what testing would settle things. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Identify the specific DMD variant in an affected male first, then test at-risk female relatives for that known variant
choices.feedback: Right. Testing an affected person defines the family variant and makes carrier testing in relatives interpretable. Testing a woman blindly risks an uninformative result.

choices.text: Test all the women first, since they are the ones making reproductive decisions
choices.feedback: Understandable priority, wrong order. Without a known family variant, a negative result in a woman may only mean the assay missed something.

choices.text: Skip genetic testing and rely on creatine kinase levels in the women
choices.feedback: Elevated creatine kinase supports carrier status but a normal level does not exclude it, so it cannot be the basis of counseling.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry out of this problem: name the inheritance mode before you compute anything, because every number depends on it. Father-to-son transmission is the single most powerful observation on a pedigree, and its absence plus male-predominant disease through unaffected women means X-linked recessive. From there the arithmetic is small. An affected son makes his mother an obligate carrier. A carrier mother gives 1/2 of sons affected and 1/2 of daughters carriers, which is 1/4 of pregnancies before you know the sex. An affected father gives every daughter the allele and no son anything. And notice the two different kinds of numbers that get confused constantly: the probability that a living adult carries an allele, and the probability that a future pregnancy is affected. Write which one the question asks before you start.

scenarios.title: Problem set: Hardy-Weinberg at the counseling table
scenarios.intro:
The case on the worksheet: a healthy `29`-year-old woman of Northern European ancestry is planning a pregnancy. Her brother has cystic fibrosis. Her partner has no family history and has not been screened.

You are given one population figure: cystic fibrosis affects about `1 in 2,500` people in this ancestry group. Everything else you have to derive.

Work the population math first, then the family math, then combine them.

steps.prompt: Start with the partner, who has no family history. What is his prior probability of being a carrier?

choices.text: Use Hardy-Weinberg: q^2 = 1/2500 so q = 0.02, and carrier frequency 2pq = 2 x 0.98 x 0.02 = 0.039, about 1 in 25
choices.feedback: Correct and fully worked. Take the square root of the disease frequency to get q, then double it (since p is near 1) to get the carrier frequency.

choices.text: It is 1 in 2,500, the same as the disease frequency
choices.feedback: That is the frequency of affected people, q^2. Carriers are far more common than affected people for any rare recessive — about 100 times more common here.

choices.text: Roughly 1 in 25, from the rule of thumb that carrier frequency is about 2 times the square root of the disease frequency
choices.feedback: Same answer by the shortcut, and the shortcut is legitimate because p is close to 1 for any rare allele. Just be ready to show the full equation if asked.

choices.text: Zero, since he has no family history
choices.feedback: Most carriers have no family history at all, which is exactly why population carrier screening exists.

steps.prompt: Now the woman. Her brother is affected, and she is not. What is her carrier probability, and why is it not the population figure?

choices.text: 1/2, since one of her parents is a carrier
choices.feedback: Both parents are obligate carriers, not one, and the correct conditioning removes a box from the square rather than halving anything.

choices.text: 2/3, because both parents are obligate carriers and being unaffected removes the aa box from AA, Aa, Aa, aa
choices.feedback: Exactly right. The prior was 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa; deleting aa leaves three equally likely boxes and two of them are carriers.

choices.text: 1 in 25, the population carrier frequency
choices.feedback: Family history beats population data every time. Her affected brother tells you far more about her than the population frequency does.

steps.prompt: Combine them. What is the chance their first child has cystic fibrosis, before any testing?

choices.feedback: Correct chain, and it is pure product rule: she is a carrier, and he is a carrier, and they both transmit. Roughly 0.67 percent.

choices.text: 1/4, since that is the risk for a carrier couple
choices.feedback: The 1/4 applies only once both parents are known carriers. Here neither is confirmed, so you must multiply by both carrier probabilities first.
Adding gives a probability larger than any single term, which should immediately look wrong. Use the sum rule only for mutually exclusive alternatives, never for a chain of conditions.

steps.prompt: The partner has carrier screening on a panel that detects about `90 percent` of variants in this population. His result is negative. What do you tell the couple?

choices.text: His risk is now essentially zero and no further discussion is needed
choices.feedback: No screen detects everything. Declaring zero risk overstates the test and is the error the concept of residual risk exists to prevent.

choices.text: His carrier risk drops substantially but not to zero; the leftover chance that he carries an undetected variant is the residual risk
choices.feedback: Correct framing. A negative on a 90 percent panel leaves roughly a tenth of the original risk, so about 1 in 250 rather than 1 in 25, and the couple's risk falls proportionally.

choices.text: The result is meaningless without testing her first
choices.feedback: Testing order can matter for efficiency, but his negative result is genuinely informative on its own. It lowers, without eliminating, his contribution to the risk.

steps.prompt: The couple then asks about their own relatedness: they are second cousins. How does consanguinity change the picture, and what do you say about it?

choices.text: It raises the chance they share a rare recessive allele inherited from a common ancestor, increasing homozygosity in offspring without changing population allele frequencies
choices.feedback: Correct mechanism. Consanguinity does not create new alleles; it makes it more likely that both copies a child receives come from the same ancestral source.

choices.text: It increases the frequency of the disease allele in the population
choices.feedback: Allele frequencies are unchanged by mating patterns. What changes is genotype distribution, with more homozygotes and fewer heterozygotes than Hardy-Weinberg predicts.

choices.text: It has no effect at all, since cystic fibrosis is common enough already
choices.feedback: The effect is modest for common recessive alleles and large for rare ones, but it is never zero. First cousins share 1/8 of their genes and second cousins about 1/32.

steps.prompt: Final item on the worksheet: the woman asks you directly whether she should have prenatal diagnostic testing. What is the appropriate counseling stance?

choices.text: Lay out her options, the risks and the detection rates, and support whichever decision she makes
choices.feedback: That is nondirective counseling, the professional standard. Your job is to make the choice informed, not to make it for her.

choices.text: Recommend amniocentesis, since her family history makes it the safest course
choices.feedback: Directive advice, and it also misstates safety: amniocentesis carries about a 1 in 400 loss risk, which is a real tradeoff she has to weigh herself.

choices.text: Suggest she first be tested for the specific variant her brother carries, then revisit the question with a sharper number
choices.feedback: A good practical sequencing suggestion. Knowing the familial variant makes her own test definitive and can remove the question entirely if she is negative.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry out of this problem: population math and family math answer different questions, and you need both. Hardy-Weinberg tells you about a stranger — take the square root of the disease frequency to get q, then double it for the carrier frequency, since p is near 1 for any rare allele. A pedigree tells you about a relative, and it always beats the population number: the unaffected sibling of an affected child is a carrier with probability 2/3, not 1/25. Combining them is the product rule, one link per condition: she carries, and he carries, and both transmit. Then remember what testing does and does not do. A negative screen scales risk down by the detection rate, it never zeroes it, and the leftover is the residual risk you are obligated to name. Consanguinity shifts genotypes toward homozygosity without touching allele frequencies. And the counseling itself stays nondirective — you supply the numbers and the options, the patient supplies the decision.
